beats.act: PROBLEM — why this is worth solving
beats.role_note: Mandatory PROBLEM beat: the stakes, stated BEFORE any prompt.
beats.narration_text: Here is the problem, before we write a line. Comparing a query against every stored vector is exactly correct — it never misses a true nearest neighbour. It is also the thing that does not scale: every comparison still has to happen, so double the collection and you double the work. A few hundred chunks is fine. A whole company's documents is not.

props.headline: Exact search doesn't scale.
props.subline: Checking every stored vector never misses the true nearest neighbour — and that is exactly why it gets slower in step with the collection. The accuracy is not the problem. The arithmetic is.

beats.narration_text: The ask: build the naive version, and time it honestly. Synthetic embeddings at three collection sizes — a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand. Twenty queries each, top ten, comparing against every single stored vector. No index, no tricks. I want to measure what exact search actually costs as the pile grows.

props.segment: Watch Exact Search Hit A Wall.
props.command: claude "write brute_force_search.py — build synthetic 384-dim embeddings at 1k, 10k and 100k, run 20 top-10 queries against each by comparing the query to EVERY stored vector, and print milliseconds per query"

beats.narration_text: Read the search function. One dot product against every stored vector, then keep the top ten. The vectors are normalised, so that dot product is cosine similarity — the measure from chapter three. There is no cleverness in here, and that is the point: this is the version that is exactly right, and we are about to watch what being exactly right costs.

props.title: brute_force_search.py — Claude Code output
props.code:
def brute_force(db, q, k=K):
    """Compare the query against EVERY stored vector. Exact — never misses."""
    sims = db @ q                      # one dot product per stored vector
    top = np.argpartition(-sims, k)[:k]
    return top[np.argsort(-sims[top])]


for n in SIZES:                        # 1_000, 10_000, 100_000
    db = make_corpus(n, rng, projection)

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for q in queries:
        brute_force(db, q)
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / N_QUERIES * 1000

    print(f"{n:>9,}  {ms:>9.2f}  {n:>15,}")

beats.narration_text: Run it. A thousand vectors: eight hundredths of a millisecond. Ten thousand: one point one six. A hundred thousand: ten point nine. Ten times the collection, and very nearly ten times the time. That is the linear curve, measured on this machine — and a real company's document store does not stop at a hundred thousand chunks.

beats.role_note: THE REVISION LAW — the second cycle begins here.
beats.narration_text: Now the revision, and notice what I am asking for. Group the vectors into cells. Compare the query against the cell centroids first, then scan only the nearest few cells. And — this is the part that matters — report recall against the exact answer, so we measure what the shortcut costs instead of assuming it is free.

props.segment: Watch Exact Search Hit A Wall.
props.command: claude "now add an inverted-file index — cluster the vectors into about sqrt(n) cells, compare the query to the centroids first, then scan ONLY the nearest few cells. Report comparisons per query AND recall@10 against the exact answer."

beats.narration_text: Two functions carry the whole idea. Build groups every vector into a cell — about the square root of the collection, so each cell holds about the square root too. Search ranks the centroids, takes the nearest few cells, and scans only what is inside them. Everything else is never examined. That is the entire trick.

props.title: ann_search.py — the index, and the search
props.code:
def n_cells(n: int) -> int:
    """~sqrt(n) cells, so each holds ~sqrt(n) vectors."""
    return max(4, int(round(n ** 0.5)))


def build_lists(db, centroids):
    """The inverted file: cell id -> the row ids that live in it."""
    assign = np.argmax(db @ centroids.T, axis=1)
    return [np.flatnonzero(assign == c) for c in range(len(centroids))]


def ivf_search(db, centroids, lists, q, nprobe, k=K):
    """Rank the cells, then scan ONLY the nearest nprobe of them."""
    near = np.argpartition(-(centroids @ q), nprobe)[:nprobe]
    cand = np.concatenate([lists[c] for c in near])   # the only rows touched
    sims = db[cand] @ q
    top = np.argpartition(-sims, k)[:k]
    return cand[top[np.argsort(-sims[top])]]

beats.narration_text: Here is what that buys. A hundred times the data: exact search goes from a thousand comparisons per query to a hundred thousand — a hundred times the work, exactly as promised. The index goes from a hundred and twenty-one to one thousand two hundred and seventy-one. Ten and a half times, for a hundred times the data. That is the chapter's figure, measured.

beats.role_note: FALSIFIABILITY — the cost of approximating, measured, not assumed.
beats.narration_text: And here is the cost, because it is not free. Compare against a third of one percent of the collection and you get a third of the true neighbours back. One and a third percent gets you sixty percent. Five percent gets you eighty-eight. Ten percent gets you ninety-six. Approximate does not mean unpredictable. It means there is a dial, and you decide where to set it.

beats.role_note: Mandatory SUMMARY beat — the lesson, in one.
beats.narration_text: So: exact search is correct and does not scale, because every comparison still has to happen. An index narrows the search space instead of scanning it, and the cost stops tracking the collection. What you pay is recall — and you pay exactly as much as you choose to. One honest caveat: the chapter walks through HNSW, a graph index. We built an inverted file. Different mechanism, same bargain.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — read aloud verbatim, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'Take my brute-force search and add an approximate index, then sweep the accuracy setting and plot recall against the share of the collection actually compared. Tell me the lowest setting that still answers my questions correctly, and show me the query where it first breaks.' That last clause is the one that earns its keep. Anything will hand you a speedup; asking for the query where it first breaks makes it show you the failure instead of averaging it away. Run it on your own data, and find your own breaking point.
